1:
Luke alone records the request, and the modern commentators divide first over why it was made. Lightfoot puts the difficulty sharply: the disciple had already been given a form in the Sermon on the Mount, so either he forgot it or wanted something else — most probably a rule like the one John gave his own followers. Wesley supplies the custom behind that: the Jewish masters gave their followers a short form of prayer as a badge of their relation to them, as John had probably done. Calvin leaves open whether Christ delivered the form once or twice, noting that Luke has him asked for it where Matthew has him teach it unprompted. Ellicott infers from the narrative and from Jewish practice that Christ prayed aloud and was overheard, and that the disciples, unable to follow, wished to pray as he prayed. Barnes and Henry both count how often Luke records Christ praying — at his baptism, in the wilderness, all night before the apostles were chosen, and at the transfiguration — Henry adding that as God he was prayed to and as man he prayed. Robertson observes that Jesus had taught the subject already by precept and example, and that this occasion revived their interest in it.

The catena asks a different question: why one who lacks nothing should pray at all. Bede sets the scene against the two sisters of the preceding chapter, who signified the two lives of the Church, and finds the prayer Christ taught containing the mystery of each, those lives being perfected by prayer and not by our own strength. Titus explains the request from the novelty of what they had seen: a new way of life asks a new form of prayer, and they wished not to sin by asking one thing instead of another, or approaching God as they ought not. Origen has the disciple point to John as the model, and takes up the first petition — that the name of God has not yet been made holy where idolaters give it to idols and creatures. Gregory of Nyssa says only that Christ unfolds the teaching to disciples who wisely desired it; Basil, whom the chain quotes next, distinguishes two kinds of prayer, one of praise with humiliation and one of petition, and warns against breaking straight into petition instead of beginning with the praise of him who created all things.

On the petitions the fathers work through the text. Pseudo-Augustine reads the first as a prayer for the cleansing of the whole world, that God’s holiness be known everywhere and worthily praised, since praise becomes the upright. Augustine handles the difference between the evangelists: Matthew appears to give seven petitions and Luke five, yet they do not disagree, Luke’s brevity showing how the seven are to be understood, since he treats the third as a repetition of the two before it and omits it. Cyril raises whether saints may ask God for bodily goods and decides they may, seeking their common bread without blame; the command to ask for daily food implies they should possess nothing, but practise an honourable poverty. Basil adds that we should not pray for bodily afflictions, since Christ told men everywhere to pray that they enter not into temptation, and that one already entered should ask for power to endure.

Gill and Tertullian mark the outer limits of the range. Gill argues these directions, though agreeing with those in Matthew, were given at another time, place and occasion — Christ was then in Galilee and is now in Judea, and gave the earlier ones unasked where these were requested. Tertullian is not expounding at all but disputing, against an opponent for whom the Father addressed here is not the Creator: he fastens on this same request and says the disciple can only have spoken so because he thought different prayers were required for different gods.
2:
Ellicott begins from the prayer being a reproduction, with only a verbal variation here and there which may well be the reporter’s, of what had already been given in the Sermon on the Mount — and finds that every way significant. What had been given to the multitude was enough for them; if earnest desires did not spontaneously clothe themselves in words, this simplest and shortest of prayers expressed everything a man should seek to ask. Wesley draws the practical consequence, that what was said to them is undoubtedly said to us also, so that we are directed not merely to imitate this in all our prayers but to use this very form. Gill notes that although one disciple asked, Christ answered them all, the request being made in the name of the rest and the instruction concerning every one of them.

Cyril of Alexandria treats the petitions as a banquet rather than a list. Those who possess earthly riches invite the friends they wish to honour and set a costly table before them, providing nothing beyond the satisfying of appetite; the Saviour feasts no one with bodily enjoyments, which are profitless and injurious even to the body, but banquets the hearts of the virtuous with the saving doctrine of the gospel. He counts the insatiate desire of learning worthy of all praise — blessed are they that hunger and thirst after righteousness — and holds that whoever would understand these words without error needs divine light, which is why David prayed to be led into God’s truth and taught. On the bread he grants that the saints should indeed strive above all for spiritual gifts, but refuses to divert the petition into a wholly spiritual sense: they may ask for simple bread, and their address to God is free from blame.

Cyril of Jerusalem comes to the prayer from the liturgy rather than the commentary. He describes the congregation saying, after all that precedes it, the prayer the Saviour delivered to his disciples, entitling God Father with a pure conscience; and the wonder is the address itself, since on those who had revolted and were in the extreme of misery God has bestowed so complete a forgiveness and so great a share of grace that they should even call him Father. On the last petition he raises the obvious objection: does Christ teach us to pray not to be tempted at all, when a man untempted is a man unproved and we are told to count it all joy when we fall into divers temptations? His answer is that entering into temptation means being overwhelmed by it — temptation is like a winter torrent hard to cross, and those who are not swept away pass through.

The remaining witnesses work at the wording. Gill records that the phrase may be rendered day by day, or for the day, or every day with the Syriac, and that Beza’s most ancient copy reads debts rather than sins, which agrees best with the indebted that follows. Barnes observes that Luke’s clause about forgiving differs from Matthew’s in form though not in sense, and states it carefully: unless we come to God really forgiving all others we cannot expect pardon, yet forgiving does not merit forgiveness — it is the disposition without which God cannot consistently pardon; those indebted are those who have injured us. Wesley adds that the forgiving is not once but continual, and that it removes a hindrance rather than supplying a meritorious cause. Lightfoot argues the petition against temptation is aimed principally at the devil’s visible apparitions and actual obsessions, which much softens the phrase about God leading us, and explains the missing doxology by Christ’s intention to deliver a form merely petitionary. Clarke follows him on both counts, and adds that deliver us from evil renders the Greek inadequately: it is deliver us from the wicked one.
5:
Cyril states the occasion: the Saviour had taught how men ought to pray, but those who received that teaching might use the form carelessly and languidly, and leave off when not heard at the first or second asking. The parable is set against exactly that, to show that cowardice in prayer is hurtful and patience in it of great advantage. Calvin, noting Matthew does not carry the comparison, reaches the same instruction: believers should not be discouraged if they do not immediately obtain their desires, since if among men importunity extorts what a man would not willingly do, there is no reason to doubt God will listen to those who persevere. Henry adds that we come as a man comes to a kind neighbour, and for bread — that is, for what is needful; if God does not answer speedily he will in due time. Wesley fastens on the hour: midnight is the most unseasonable time, but no time is unseasonable with God, either for hearing or for answering.

Ellicott declines to call it a parable at all. The illustration is peculiar to Luke; its familiar tone, appealing to each man’s natural good-will, and the dramatic vividness of the dialogue make it almost unique in our Lord’s teaching. Midnight is the hour at which above all others men expect to be left to their repose; the three loaves are one for the host, one for the guest, one in reserve, and the scene is a poor man’s single room. He warns that the illustrative matter cannot be pressed into an interpretation, being framed to suggest only an argument from lesser to greater: thus a man might answer, but so does not God. Barnes agrees the design is solely importunity, and defines it as troublesome perseverance refusing any denial — an improper perseverance, the sleeper being moved simply to avoid further disturbance. Ellicott adds that the Greek means literally shamelessness and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; Robertson confirms it, notes the verb for lending is the friendly loan and not the loan at interest and likewise occurs only here, renders the refusal “stop furnishing troubles to me,” and marks the perfect tense of the shut door — shut to stay shut.

The catena reads the scene allegorically and does not agree with itself. Gloss holds the difficulty of obtaining is meant not to take away the liberty of asking but to kindle the desire of praying. Ambrose takes the shut door for the one Paul asked to have opened to him, seeking the people’s prayers as well as his own that a door of utterance might be given him to speak the mystery of Christ, and perhaps the door John saw open. Augustine reads the midnight as a famine of the word, when understanding is shut up and those who dealt out the wisdom of the gospel like bread are at rest with the Lord — which the children in bed signify; Gregory of Nyssa, quoted next, takes them for such as have won freedom from passion by the arms of righteousness. Theophylact offers two readings and commits to neither: either the midnight is the end of life, at which many come to God, and the friend the angel who receives the soul; or it is the depth of temptation, the three loaves relief for body, soul and spirit, and the friend arriving from a journey God himself, who tries men by temptations.

Gill and Clarke both press the traveller’s plight — out of the way, benighted, having lost his road — which Clarke thinks a strong reason for prompt relief; Clarke also prefers Bishop Pearce’s rendering, I and my children are in bed. Gill notes the Vulgate premises to the last verse the words if he continue knocking; Barnes, finding them absent from the Greek, holds them indispensable, since knocking once would not be importunity at all.
9:
Augustine marks the transition: the metaphor laid aside, our Lord adds a plain exhortation to ask, seek and knock until we receive what we seek. Cyril takes “I say unto you” to carry the force of an oath — God does not lie, and when he confirms a thing with an oath he exposes the inexcusable littleness of our faith. Chrysostom, quoted next, distinguishes the verbs: asking is prayer, seeking is zeal and anxiety, since what is sought requires great care, peculiarly so with God, because many things block up our senses — as we search for lost gold, so let us seek God. Ambrose supplies the logic of the promise: one who promises ought to convey a hope of it, so obedience may follow the command and faith the promise.

The obvious objection is raised inside the chain itself. Origen asks how it comes that those who pray are not heard, and answers that whoever seeks in the right way, omitting nothing that avails toward obtaining, really does receive what he prayed for; the failure lies in turning away from the object of a right request. Basil sharpens this: a man who from indolence surrenders to his desires and betrays himself into his enemies’ hands is neither assisted nor heard, having alienated himself by sin; and one who asks slackly, with a mind wavering to and fro, will provoke God to anger rather than obtain. Gill says the same in his own terms: some ask and do not receive because they ask amiss — wrong person, wrong manner, wrong principles, wrong ends; where the object, matter, manner and end are right, a man has his petitions however mean he is, not by deserts but by the riches of grace. Clarke turns the importunity inward: be importunate not so much to prevail on God to save you as to bring yourself into a disposition to receive the mercy he is always ready to give, since one who is not importunate does not feel his need.

On the three pairs the fathers read symbol where the moderns read natural history. Augustine takes the bread for charity, which we desire most and without which all else is nothing, the stone opposed to it for hardness of heart, and the fish for belief in things invisible. Origen makes the bread the soul’s food in knowledge, the well-planned rule of a just life, and the fish the love of instruction. Gill, by contrast, catalogues the scorpion: some are land scorpions, a venomous kind of serpent; some flying, a sort of fowl; some of the sea and of the fish kind, and it is not easy to say which is meant. Barnes reports Dr. Thomson’s observation that no likeness exists between an egg and the ordinary black scorpion, but that old writers describe a white one which, with its tail folded, would not look unlike a small egg. Clarke reasons from the other cases: eels closely resemble serpents and some stones exactly resemble bread, so a similitude between egg and scorpion is what our Lord intended. Robertson notes only that the sentence breaks its construction.

The close draws unanimous notice because Luke differs from Matthew. Ellicott observes that the one highest gift of the Holy Spirit replaces the wider and less definite good things, and thinks the variation significant as belonging to a later stage of the teaching and as spoken probably to some of the Seventy, taught to ask boldly for the Spirit. Robertson marks the same substitution; Wesley the ascent behind it — a friend, a father, God — calling the Spirit the best of gifts and the one including every good gift. Clarke records that several manuscripts read the good spirit instead. Cyril of Jerusalem cites the verse as his proof that this grace comes from the Father, setting it beside the words about being born of water and of the Spirit.
14:
Gloss ties the miracle to what precedes: the Lord had promised the Holy Spirit to those who asked, and the blessed effects of that gift are shown at once in what follows. Theophylact takes up the word for dumb, which commonly means one who does not speak but is also used of one who does not hear, and most properly of one who neither hears nor speaks — and he notes the reason the two go together, since a man who has not heard from birth necessarily cannot speak, we speaking only what we have been taught. Bede brings in the other evangelist: Matthew reports the man blind as well as dumb, so that three miracles were done at once upon one man, the blind seeing, the dumb speaking, and the possessed set free. He then makes the whole a picture of conversion, which daily accomplishes the same: the devil is first cast out, the light is seen, and mouths that were silent are loosed to speak the praises of God. Cyril, quoted after him, notes that when the miracle was done the multitude extolled him aloud.

Henry states the argument the miracle carries. Christ is here giving a general proof of his divine mission by a particular proof of his power over Satan, and his conquest of him indicates the great design of his coming into the world, which was to destroy the works of the devil; the cure is an earnest of that undertaking’s success. Wesley makes the small but exact point that the spirit was dumb in the sense that it made the man so. Gill accounts for the reaction: the Pharisees could not bear that Christ should be thought the Messiah, and so put an ill construction on the miracle, while the others who tempted him were Scribes and Pharisees, or else Sadducees. Robertson agrees that denial was not open to them — it was useless to deny the fact of the miracles, so they were explained as wrought by Satan himself, which he calls a most absurd explanation, and he observes that the charge is made here in Judea exactly as it had been in Galilee.

The name itself is disputed. Lightfoot insists on reading it with a final letter l — Beelzebul — against the Syriac, Persian, Vulgate and other versions which give Beelzebub, and remarks that the Italian hedges with a form that commits to neither, for whose candour he declines to answer. Wesley takes the other reading and glosses it: Beelzebub signifies the lord of flies, a title the heathen gave to Jupiter, whom they reckoned chief of their gods and yet supposed to be employed in driving flies from their temple and sacrifices, and under which name the Philistines worshipped the god of Ekron.

On the demand for a sign the two commentators who treat it agree about the motive. Robertson holds that these others had grasped the futility of the Beelzebub charge and shifted ground, asking for the kind of spectacular display of heavenly power they expected of the Messiah — the same thing the devil had proposed on the pinnacle of the temple — and he notes that the tense shows them keeping on at it rather than asking once. Calvin observes that Matthew and Mark record a like demand later, which shows Christ was attacked repeatedly on this point and that there was no end to the wickedness of men who had once resolved to oppose the truth; and he reads the request as a manoeuvre, since they ask for a sign in order to plead as a plausible pretext for their unbelief that his calling had not been duly attested.
17:
Chrysostom sets the scene: the suspicion was so unreasonable that the Pharisees dared not divulge it for fear of the multitude, and only turned it over in their minds. Bede draws the consequence — Christ answered not their words but their thoughts, so they might be compelled to believe in the power of one who saw the heart’s secrets — and Gill puts it flatly, that he knew their thoughts as God omniscient. Robertson notes the word for their thinking means intent or purpose and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Ambrose reads the maxim two ways at once: it shows Christ’s kingdom undivided and everlasting, while those who think he casts out devils by the chief of the devils have a kingdom that is not — which he applies to the Jewish people, asking how their kingdom can stand when by the people of the law Jesus is denied whom the law promised.

On the argument from their own exorcists the witnesses agree. Bede takes the sons of the Jews for that nation’s exorcists, who cast out devils by invoking God: if their work is ascribed to God and not to devils, why has not the same work the same cause in Christ’s case? They judge not by authority but in act, assigning to God what their fathers assign to Beelzebub. Robertson observes the sentence is a first-class condition, so Jesus assumes the charge for argument’s sake, and that Jewish exorcists practised incantations. Gill adds that the Greek copies spell the name with a final l.

The finger of God draws most comment, Matthew having the Spirit of God instead. Cyril concludes from the calumny itself that he plainly casts out devils by the Spirit of God; Augustine, quoted next, holds the two phrases do not disturb the evangelists’ agreement. Ellicott traces the expression — the prophets’ hand of the Lord for the state issuing in inspiration, the finger that wrote the commandments on stone, and Pharaoh’s confession of it with Moses and Aaron. Robertson notes the phrase stands in distinction from the Jewish exorcists. Gill reports the Cabalistic Jews explain it as the power of God; Wesley takes it as a power manifestly divine, thinks it may intimate the work cost no labour, and adds the kingdom comes unawares.

The chain expounds the strong man almost line by line. Cyril says our Lord uses a very plain example to prove he overcomes the power of the world by a power inherent in himself. Chrysostom qualifies the title: the devil is called strong not because he is so by nature but with reference to his ancient dominion, of which our weakness was the cause. Theophylact makes his arms all kinds of sins, in which he trusted and prevailed; Bede makes the palace the world, lying in wickedness, where until the Saviour’s coming he held supreme power, resting unopposed in unbelievers’ hearts. Basil reads the dividing of the spoil as the watch angels keep over men’s salvation; Bede as the sign of triumph, since leading captivity captive he gave gifts to men and ordained apostles, evangelists, prophets and teachers. Gill arms him with his own temptations, thrown thick and fast like fiery darts, and with the sins of men, armour of unrighteousness turned back upon them; Wesley more briefly with the pride, obstinacy and security of the man he dwells in. Robertson notes the participle is perfect and found only here, the palace is really a homestead, and the guarding is continuous where the assault is a single onset. Chrysostom counts the last verse the fourth answer — Christ would present men to God and Satan the contrary, so one who scatters what is Christ’s could hardly join him in casting out devils — and Gill denies it condemns everyone not personally in Christ’s company, since many not with him in person were not against him.
24:
The chain reads the whole passage as an account of one nation rather than of one man, and says so openly. Cyril explains that our Lord is showing how the Jewish people came by their opinions concerning Christ, and appeals to Matthew, who closes the same saying with the words about this wicked generation. On his reading, all the time they lived in Egypt after the Egyptian manner an evil spirit dwelt in them, and it was drawn out when they sacrificed the lamb as a type of Christ. Ambrose states the comparison as one between a single man and the whole people, from whom the unclean spirit had been cast out by the Law; the spirit finds no rest among the Gentiles, whose hearts were barren at first but afterwards moistened in baptism with the dew of the Spirit, because to unclean spirits Christ is a flaming fire, and so it returns to the house it came from, Israel being adorned with a merely outward ornament. Origen makes the same identification of the empty house: it is those of Israel in whom the spirit saw nothing divine, but a place desolate and vacant for him to take up his abode.

Chrysostom carries the reading to its end and dates it. The evil spirits now dwelling in those souls are worse than the former ones, because formerly they raged against the prophets and now lift their hands against the Lord of the prophets; and so, he argues, they suffered worse at the hands of Vespasian and Titus than they had in Egypt or in Babylon. Where once they had the providence of God and the grace of the Holy Spirit with them, they are now deprived even of that protection. Wesley arrives at the same historical application from a different direction, appealing to the account Josephus gives of the temple and the conduct of the people between the ascension and the final destruction by the Romans: no emblem, he says, could describe them better, since they pressed on to their own ruin as though possessed by legions of devils and wrought up to the last degree of madness. He then widens it, holding that the same is fulfilled in all who totally and finally fall away.

Bede alone declines the national reading and offers something simpler. The words may be understood as added to mark the distinction between Satan’s works and Christ’s: Christ is ever hastening to cleanse what has been defiled, and Satan to defile with still greater pollution what has been cleansed. Gill likewise keeps the saying general and applies it to a false profession. The unclean spirit works in the children of disobedience, whether they profess religion or not, and delights to dwell where hearts are unclean like himself; he may be said to go out in appearance when a man outwardly reforms and takes up a profession. On the swept and garnished house Gill argues that it is empty of all goodness for all the sweeping, notes that Matthew and the Arabic add the word empty and the Ethiopic reads empty of men, and records the Persic rendering, heated and prepared — heated with wrath and fury against Christ and his gospel, and so fitted to be a proper habitation for Satan. The seven he takes as consorts and companions.

Robertson confines himself to the comparison of the texts. The three verses are almost verbatim what Matthew has, with three differences he lists: Luke uses a participle where Matthew has an indicative for the finding of no rest; Matthew has the spirit take the others with himself where Luke has him simply take them; and Luke omits the closing sentence about this evil generation altogether. He notes the comparative in the last clause, and that the seven demons brought back recall the seven from which Mary Magdalene was delivered.
27:
Every witness notices the timing. Bede sets the interruption against what surrounds it: while the Scribes and Pharisees were tempting our Lord and uttering blasphemies, a woman with great boldness confessed his incarnation, and by doing so refuted at once the calumnies of the rulers present and the unbelief of later heretics — for as the Jews then denied the true Son of God by blaspheming the works of the Holy Spirit, so afterwards heretics would deny his birth of the Virgin. Gill makes the same connection more plainly, that she spoke as Christ finished the sayings by which he had vindicated himself and his miracles from the blasphemy of the Scribes and Pharisees. Henry, who notes the passage is in no other evangelist and declines to attach it to the earlier scene with Christ’s mother and brethren, calls her an affectionate, honest, well-meaning woman — probably a person of some quality — who admired the discourses that the scribes despised and blasphemed.

On what she meant the readings differ. Barnes takes her simply to have thought that the mother of such a person must be peculiarly happy. Clarke calls the exclamation very natural for a woman who was probably herself a mother. Calvin insists that her intention was to magnify Christ and not Mary, whom she had perhaps never seen — though he grants the blessing was not inappropriate, since scripture does declare offspring, and especially offspring endued with distinguished virtues, to be a remarkable gift of God. Ellicott and Robertson both hear an echo instead: the words are the first direct fulfilment of the Magnificat, that all generations shall call her blessed, and Robertson adds that the woman’s beatitude recalls Elisabeth’s greeting. Ellicott notes that the incident is peculiar to Luke and seems to have reached him from the company of devout women he came into contact with; Robertson, calling this in a special sense the Gospel of Woman, quotes the judgment that she speaks well, but womanly.

The reply is read by all as correction without rebuke, and the witnesses differ only in emphasis. Gill notes that Christ neither denied what she said nor reproved her for it, but improved upon it. Barnes has him admit that she was happy and that it was an honour to be his mother, while insisting the chief happiness and highest honour is to obey the word of God, against which all earthly distinctions are nothing. Chrysostom puts it as a disclaimer of nothing: he did not seek to disown his mother but to show that his birth would have profited her nothing had she not been really fruitful in works and faith — and if it profited Mary nothing to have borne him without the inward virtue of her heart, much less will a virtuous father, brother or son avail us while we ourselves are strangers to virtue. Wesley compresses the same argument into a sentence, that if even she who bore him had not heard and kept the word she would have forfeited all her blessedness. Clarke draws the pastoral conclusion, that the holy virgin could not be benefited merely by being mother of his human nature, and that they only are happy who carry Christ in their hearts.

Two further notes bear on the wording. Ellicott holds that the word of God here designates the message of the kingdom as our Lord himself spoke it, and that although the phrase in its wider use includes the written record of that word and of later revelations, it must not be confined to them. Robertson observes that Christ turns the attention away from himself to others and gives them a beatitude of their own, and reports the view that the originality of the reply guarantees its historical character, being beyond the reach of an inventor.
29:
Bede marks the turn: our Lord had been assailed with two kinds of question, the charge of casting out devils by Beelzebub, answered until now, and the demand for a sign from heaven, answered here. Robertson catches the setting in the verb, a rare word found only here in the New Testament and meaning to throng together. Gill suggests they gathered either at the woman’s outcry or, more likely, to see what sign he would give. Wesley notes the word for seeking implies seeking more than one has already, which is Henry’s complaint: the demand is reproved because signs had been given in great plenty. Henry adds what the sign still to come would be: the most convincing proof of Christ’s being sent of God was to be his resurrection.

On the sign of Jonah the witnesses agree in substance and differ in use. Calvin observes the word is not taken in its ordinary sense of pointing something out but of what lies far outside the course of nature, Jonah’s mission being miraculous when he was brought from the fish’s belly as if from the grave. Gill describes it the same way and notes its purpose, to confirm the prophet’s mission so the Ninevites would credit him and repent. Ambrose makes it at once a type of our Lord’s passion and a testimony of grievous sin, so the passage carries both a warning and a declaration of mercy: by the Ninevites’ example a punishment is denounced and a remedy promised, and these hearers need not despair of pardon if they will repent. Theophylact adds that Jonah, after coming out of the whale, converted the men of the city. Cyril of Jerusalem puts the text to another use, meeting the objection that though a body lately dead has been raised, none has shown that one three days dead can rise; the proof, he says, Christ supplies himself in this saying. Robertson notes that Luke, unlike Matthew, does not here spell out the burial and resurrection of which Jonah’s experience was the type.

Two textual observations follow. Augustine faces the different order of the sayings in the two evangelists and dismisses it: an idle question, since no one repeats another’s words in the order they were spoken, and the order makes no difference to the fact. Gill notices the same reversal in the two examples, Matthew placing Nineveh first and Luke last, and calls it immaterial; Robertson observes that Luke inserts the queen between the halves of the Jonah saying, and that Matthew writes simply “with this generation” where Luke writes “with the men of this generation.”

On the two witnesses from outside Israel the notes are particular. Gill identifies the queen of the south as the queen of Sheba, a country of Arabia lying south of Judea. Lightfoot records his puzzlement at the saying in Bava Bathra that whoever calls the queen of Sheba a woman is mistaken, the kingdom being meant — asking whether the whole kingdom of the Sabeans came to Solomon. Clarke would rather render both sayings indefinitely, a queen of the south and the men of this race. Wesley presses the Nineveh comparison furthest: the Ninevites repented only for a season and relapsed until, about forty years later, they were destroyed — and the comparison holds, these hearers being likewise reprieved some forty years and still advancing in wickedness until their measure was full. Tertullian is again arguing rather than expounding, and turns the refusal of a sign against his opponents’ own Christ: it is enough, he says, that the faults the Marcionites find in the Creator are found in him too, since he enjoins giving to everyone that seeks and yet refuses to give to those who seek a sign.
33:
Lightfoot admits the coherence with what precedes is a little difficult, and proposes a connection: two objections had been raised, that Christ cast out devils by the prince of the devils and that he show a sign from heaven, and this answers both, chiefly the second. Cyril gives the charge it refutes: the Jews alleged he wrought miracles not that men should believe but to gain applause and followers. Bede takes the candle for Christ speaking of himself, since though no sign was to be given but the sign of Jonas, his brightness was not for concealing. Clarke reads the figure the other way: to work a miracle among a people determined to disbelieve every evidence of his mission would be to light a candle and cover it with a bushel, defeating the end for which it was lit. Gill takes the candle for the free and open ministry of Christ, who excelled Solomon in wisdom and Jonas in preaching, and notes the saying is repeated on different occasions. Robertson observes the word for the secret place means a crypt and occurs only here in the New Testament.

On the eye the witnesses agree on the analogy and divide on its object. Theophylact states it plainly: as the body is light when the eye is light and dark when it is dark, so with the understanding in relation to the soul. Gill says the same, that the understanding is the light of the soul and guide of all its faculties, and records that the Vulgate and eastern versions read the light of thy body is thine eye. Origen makes singleness native to the understanding, which from its beginning desires only what contains no dissimulation, guile or division; Chrysostom presses what follows when that faculty is corrupted. Gregory takes a different line, reading the body as each particular action, which follows its own intention: the deserving parts of an action receive their light from the ray of a good intention, so that if we intend rightly in singleness of heart we accomplish a good work even where it does not appear to be one. Lightfoot supplies the idiom, that our Saviour speaks of the eye after the manner of the schools, where the evil eye, or the eye not single, denoted the covetous, envious and malicious mind. Wesley makes the single eye a matter of aim: God gives this gospel light that men may repent, and one who aims only at pleasing him will be full of wisdom, holiness and happiness, while one who aims at anything else will be full of folly, sin and misery.

Two comparisons with Matthew close it. Ellicott finds Luke’s sequence different and in some respects closer, since in the Sermon on the Mount the disciples are themselves the light, and the teaching about the light of the body is separated from that illustration by the comment on scribal tradition. On the warning he prefers “see to it whether the light that is in thee be darkness,” standing where Matthew has the exclamation about how great that darkness is, and reads it as a call to self-scrutiny: men must examine their primary beliefs and their intuitions of right and wrong, lest all they do be vitiated at its source. Robertson notes the construction of that indirect question is good Greek, and calls it a pitiful situation when the very light is darkness — when the eye of the soul is too diseased to see the light of Christ. Clarke records that the last two verses are missing from some manuscripts and variously read in others, and explains the final one by the completeness of vision: when the eye is perfect every object within reach is as completely seen as if there were an eye in every part, so the light of Christ dwelling fully in the heart reaches every thought, word and action.
37:
Cyril notes the invitation came while our Lord was still speaking, and Bede presses the phrasing: Luke says so to show he had not finished but was interrupted. Robertson agrees the construction means in the speaking rather than after he had spoken, against Plummer. Barnes suggests the host had felt the force of the rebukes and wished to be alone with him. Clarke and Ellicott explain the meal: the word denotes the day’s first eating, the Jews making two meals only, the chief being supper after the heat of the day. Henry sets the scene against the public discourse in the temple: Christ said much the same at a private table, since what he said in public and private was of a piece, and he would not say in a corner what he durst not repeat in the congregation.

The offence turns on how much was washed. Ellicott holds the word implies actual immersion, or at least a process taking in the whole body. Lightfoot doubts it: had the Pharisee washed his whole body before dinner? Hardly credible, since neither need nor custom required more than the hands. Robertson takes the verb as dipping and applies it to the hands. Augustine reports that they washed daily before dinner as if that could cleanse the heart, and that the host uttered no word but thought within himself — and was heard by one who perceives the heart’s secrets.

On the rebuke, Lightfoot argues from the words that persons and not vessels are meant, since your inward parts cannot be said of a cup. Calvin distinguishes this reproof from Matthew’s: Christ does not charge them with breaking God’s law for their traditions, but glances at their hypocrisy in desiring purity only before the eyes of men. Barnes takes ravening as robbery and plunder, the vessels being filled with what had been unjustly taken — a charge pressed on the very man who had invited him. Ambrose reads the vessel as the body, a fragile thing broken by a short fall, and notes that what the mind meditates within it expresses through the senses, as what a cup holds glitters outside. Ellicott observes that these are words actually repeated from the great discourse against the Pharisees, not a narrative misplaced.

The last two verses are peculiar to Luke, and divide the witnesses. Ellicott reads the question about the Maker as a latent parable: the ceremonial law ordering the outside cleansed and the moral law requiring truth within have the same Author, neither to be neglected for the other. Clarke argues from the vessel’s purpose: its maker formed it inside and out to serve an end it cannot serve if the inside is foul. Lightfoot notes that fools was a word very common in the nation. On the alms Chrysostom takes the command straight: what is enjoined is almsgiving, not injury; it makes all things clean and excels fasting, which is more painful but less profitable. Calvin agrees that Christ withdraws them from ceremonies to charity, since it is not water but liberality that cleanses men and food; Cyprian, that the merciful bids us show mercy, so that those defiled after baptism may be cleansed again. Bede limits the command to what is over and above necessary food and clothing, no one being commended for giving so as to consume himself by want. Wesley reads it as a demonstration: acts contrary to rapine show the heart cleansed and the washings needless. Barnes puts the hardest construction on it: the property is theirs though unjustly gained, and giving it to the poor is how repentance may be shown. Gill finds the phrase variously rendered and the received sense odd, since none can give what he has not; Robertson admits the expression occurs nowhere else and is unclear; and Lightfoot suspects the sentence is ironical, spoken in derision of their opinion about alms.
42:
Gill opens with the question that governs the whole section: although these woes and several other passages in this chapter closely resemble those in Matthew, it is clear they were spoken at different times, these in the house of a Pharisee and those in the temple at Jerusalem. Ellicott argues the same independence from the wording itself, listing the minor variations — rue and all manner of herbs where Matthew has anise and cummin, judgment and the love of God where Matthew has the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy and faith — and holds them sufficient to show that the two reports are independent. Robertson confirms the differences term by term: the verb for tithing is a late one meaning to take a tenth off; rue is a botanical word used by later writers, named from its thick leaves, where Matthew has anise; the phrase for every herb is general where Matthew has cummin; and where Matthew says they have left the weightier matters undone, Luke has a verb meaning to go by or beside them. Barnes describes the plant itself, a small garden herb used as a medicine, with a rosy flower, a bitter penetrating taste and a strong smell. Wesley fixes the sense of the refrain, that the woe means simply “miserable are you,” and says the phrase is to be understood so throughout the chapter.

On the second woe the notes are brief. Gill adds the uppermost rooms at feasts to the uppermost seats in the synagogues; Clarke observes that every one of them affected to be a ruler there; and Robertson explains what the seats were, a semi-circular bench that faced the congregation, noting that Luke has the singular where Matthew has the plural.

The third woe turns on a figure that is not quite Matthew’s, and both Clarke and Ellicott say so. Clarke points out that in Matthew the Pharisees are told they resemble whitewashed tombs, fair only on the outside, whereas here they are like hidden graves, marked by no outward decoration and not raised above the ground, so that men walking over them never consider what corruption lies within — and so they, under the veil of hypocrisy, covered their iniquities from those who had dealings with them. Ellicott makes the same distinction: the comparison is drawn from the same object but presents a different phase of it, the contrast in Matthew being between the whitened surface and the decaying bones, while here the whitewash has worn away and there is nothing left to distinguish the graves at all. He adds that the better manuscripts give simply “Woe unto you, Pharisees,” without the scribes and the charge of hypocrisy; Gill notes the same textual question from the other side, that the fuller address is what Matthew uses throughout and appears in Luke only here, that the Vulgate reduces the clause to the bare woe, and that the whole is retained in all the Oriental versions.
45:
Cyril observes that a reproof which exalts the meek is hateful to the proud, so the lawyers were struck with consternation when the Pharisees were blamed; Cyril of Alexandria, whose commentary on these verses stands beside that catena excerpt, makes the same point, that reproof profits the soberminded but hardens those set against admonition. Bede adds that a conscience is in a grievous state when it hears the word of God and takes it for a reproach against itself. Theophylact distinguishes the parties: the Pharisees had the appearance of a sect, while those skilled in the Law were the Doctors who resolved legal questions. Gill holds Scribes and lawyers were the same men, and Wesley calls them expounders of the law. Barnes admits it is not known how the lawyers differed from the scribes. Robertson calls the verb a positive insult; Clarke observes that only he who searches the heart could unmask such men, and did it so effectually that their consciences echoed the reproach. Lightfoot notes the preceding woe addressed scribes and Pharisees while the answer comes from a lawyer, and suspects the Vulgate dropped the words for that reason.

On the burdens the reproach is unanimous, its object disputed. Bede reads them as the Law the lawyers pretend to keep and pass on, fulfilled by them at no point. Lightfoot argues the burdens are traditions rather than the Law, everything reproached here being traditional, and Clarke agrees they insisted on the elders’ traditions while paying little attention to them. Gregory of Nyssa widens it into a standing type: many severe judges of sinners are weak combatants, imposers of laws who bear none, unwilling to approach strictness of life though exacting it from those under them. Robertson notes the word for grievous to be borne stands alone here in the critical text.

On the sepulchres, Ambrose calls the reply a good answer to a foolish superstition: those who build the prophets’ tombs condemn their fathers’ deeds and then throw the sentence back on themselves by rivalling their wickedness, since not the building but the imitation is counted a crime. Robertson calls the reasoning subtle but just, the building looking like disapproval where the reality is opposition. Clarke says they will prove by their conduct toward Christ and his apostles that they have not degenerated; Wesley, that they feign reverence for ancient prophets while destroying those sent to themselves. Ellicott prefers “truly are ye witnesses, and ye allow,” taking allow to mean approving of and having pleasure in.

The last woes turn on three phrases. Barnes takes the wisdom of God for the Saviour himself, since what follows is nowhere in the Old Testament, and Clarke thinks the words Luke’s own; Robertson doubts Jesus would so describe himself; Wesley finds the substance elsewhere in scripture though not in these words; Lightfoot and Gill compare the Jewish habit of making a divine attribute speak. On the blood, Ellicott notes the variation from Matthew’s all the righteous blood; Gill explains Abel is named as the first man slain, and for his righteousness; Clarke argues the particle means so that, marking event not design; Wesley reads the requiring as punishment; Athan observes that killing makes the blood cry the louder, since no one flees from the merciful but from the cruel. On Zacharias the Greek Exposition preserves another account: when the children were murdered John was to have died with those of his age, but Elizabeth carried him to the desert, and Herod’s soldiers, failing to find them, killed his father as he ministered. Augustine takes the key of knowledge for the humility of Christ, which they would neither understand nor let others understand; Ambrose extends the charge to all who usurp the teaching of divine knowledge, hinder others and do not acknowledge what they profess, and notes Matthew places all this after our Lord entered Jerusalem while Luke relates it here.
53:
The closing scene is read as the collapse of the dinner into open hostility, and the witnesses differ over where it takes place. Ellicott reports that the better manuscripts open the sentence with words meaning that Jesus had gone forth from thence, as though he had left the house after the last woe and was followed out by the crowd of angry and embittered disputants. Robertson agrees, taking the phrase to mean out of the Pharisee’s house, and remarks drily that we are not told what became of the breakfast, only that the rage of both Pharisees and lawyers knew no bounds. Clarke argues on other grounds that the whole conversation cannot have passed at table, since the parallel in Matthew shows the words were spoken on another occasion, and holds that the questioners had found themselves completely unmasked before a vast concourse of people. Calvin goes further and treats the arrangement as Luke’s: the preceding sentences were not inserted in their proper place, since while relating that Christ reproved the scribes at a dinner the evangelist has brought in also the latest discourses, delivered shortly before his death — though Calvin adds that he has no great objection if anyone prefers the opinion that Christ repeated the same discourses on various occasions. Gill keeps to the plain connection, that this followed his denouncing the woes and threatening them with divine vengeance.

On the manner of the attack the language does most of the work. Robertson explains the first verb as meaning to hold in, to be enraged at, to have it in for someone, and notes it is the same word used of the relentless hatred of Herodias for John the Baptist. The second he traces to a root meaning the mouth, a word used by Plato of repeating something to a pupil for him to recite from memory; Ellicott gives its force as causing a man to speak impromptu, without thought, and judges the English rendering a happy one. Barnes describes the tactic itself: they put many questions on many matters without allowing time to answer, asking as fast and as widely as they could, in the hope that in the hurry he would say something wrong — which he calls a remarkable instance of their cunning, malignity and unfairness. Clarke describes the same design, that by the multitude and impertinence of their questions they hoped to puzzle or irritate him into speaking rashly.

The last verse supplies two metaphors and both are pressed. Barnes says the phrase means laying snares rather than lying in wait, and compares men who catch birds by deceiving them and taking them unawares; the purpose was to accuse him before the great council of the nation and so secure his death. Robertson finds the figure in the words themselves — one from a root meaning a seat, hence to lie in ambush, and one belonging to the chase, to ensnare or catch in hunting — and says the two together give a vivid picture of rabbis treating Jesus as if he were a beast of prey. Gill puts it simply as watching his words to entangle him. Ellicott notes that the better manuscripts give the clause in a simpler form, and draws a consequence beyond this chapter: the words throw light on the later question about paying tribute to Caesar and show it to have been the acting out of a pre-concerted policy. Barnes closes with the lesson he draws from the whole, that faithful reproof must be expected to excite opposition and hatred, since rousing a man’s conscience against himself does not prevent his hating both the reproof and the reprover.
